title: ר' חנניה בן תירדיון

paragraphs: (a) Avot, chapter 3. In Mishnah Taanit 2:5, at Sikhni. Rosh Hashanah 27a; Taanit 16b; Sanhedrin 32b.

(b) One of the ten martyrs killed by the government, when Betar was conquered, after R. Akiva was killed. Emek HaMelekh, 40a, apparently has him killed before R. Yishmael ben Elisha. Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayyim, section יתק״פ [source form], says: on 25 Sivan R. Yishmael, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and R. Chanina, deputy of the priests, were killed; on the 26th, R. Chanina ben Teradyon was burned. When R. Yosi ben Kisma died (see there), they seized him for gathering public assemblies to study Torah. He was not saved because he engaged only in Torah; see R. Elazar ben Perata. Although he administered charity and his Purim money became mixed with charity money, which he replaced from his own, he nevertheless did not act as he ought; see Avodah Zarah, chapter 1, 17b. Concerning that deed, he was told he would merit the world to come. At the end of tractate Kallah: the executioner lit the fire, but it cooled and withdrew from him. The executioner was greatly alarmed and asked, “Rabbi, why does the fire increase?” He replied, “I adjured it by my Creator's name not to touch me until I know whether it was decreed in heaven.” He waited an hour, etc. See Yuchasin in its sequence of generations, and Shalshelet HaKabbalah, 29a and 30a, near the end; there are scribal errors there. I will therefore transcribe what Emek HaMelekh, 40a, writes, and you will understand how to correct it: “R. Yishmael the high priest said: Suriel, Prince of the Presence, told me: ‘My friend, I tell you: all shame, humiliation, and disgrace befell that wicked Lupinus. The Holy One, blessed be He, commanded destructive angels to descend and utterly destroy Lupinus's household. No survivor or fugitive remained in his palace. His youthful wife, his maidservants, and his concubines were burned; all his sons and the delights of his eyes lay before him. They terrified him greatly through his household lying before him. When people came to take one of Lupinus's dead to bury him, the abyss swallowed him; once they let go of him, the abyss cast him out. They lay before him and putrefied and stank throughout his royal palace. He was ashamed before all the princes of kingdoms who entered and left his presence. All this shame and humiliation befell that wicked man on account of R. Chananyah ben Teradyon, whose day of execution had arrived. They told him, “Reconsider concerning that sage, so he will not be killed.” He said, “Let me and all these members of my household die; let all Gappim perish by his hand, but in this matter I will not reconsider,” etc.’ R. Yishmael said: Suriel, Prince of the Presence, told me: ‘My friend, I tell you what Zohariel, God of Israel, did at that hour. He commanded me to descend. I went down and drove Lupinus from his palace as he slept at night, and took him to the prison where R. Chanina ben Teradyon had been, to tend pigs and dogs. I brought R. Chanina ben Teradyon into his palace; he had been sitting and telling wonders in the study house and teaching Torah to my fellow Israelites. I exchanged the appearance of their faces. Lupinus appeared to them like R. Chananyah ben Teradyon, and he and R. Nechunya ben HaKanah cut off his head. R. Chanina's wife [was exchanged] with Lupinus's wife, and his daughter with R. Chananyah ben Teradyon's daughter [the source's difficult formulation]. R. Chananyah ben Teradyon bound on the royal crown and ruled wicked Gappim in Lupinus's likeness for six months. He killed six thousand tzeriftami there, one thousand each month’”—Shalshelet HaKabbalah has six thousand governors—“‘and afterward he and his colleagues ascended alive in holiness and purity. They set Lupinus in R. Chanina ben Teradyon's likeness before wicked Gappim, who seized him and cast him into the fire instead of R. Chananyah ben Teradyon. But had they not cut off his head? After killing him, the heavenly court brought him back to life, and they seized him and cast him into the fire.’” See there. You can see how to correct Sefer Yuchasin, which writes: “In Sefer Heikhalot they said: when Emperor Lupinus burned R. Chananyah ben Teradyon, Emperor Lupinus appeared like R. Nechunya ben HaKanah, and they cut off his head. Afterward the heavenly court revived Lupinus, who was in R. Chananyah ben Teradyon's likeness, and they burned him as though burning R. Chanina ben Teradyon. A miracle occurred: R. Nechunya ben HaKanah appeared like Lupinus and ruled Rome for six months, killing six thousand governors. On 21 Sivan”—see above—“they burned R. Chananyah ben Teradyon, and afterward R. Yeshavav the scribe.” End of quotation. Shalshelet HaKabbalah writes: “R. Chananyah ben Teradyon was exchanged with the emperor and was emperor for six months; his princes accused him and burned him.” End of quotation. Your eyes can surely see the confused account and omissions.

(c) His wife was killed because she did not protest his teaching the Name to his students publicly. Rashi explains that he used the forty-two-letter Name. His daughter was assigned to a brothel. Beruryah, R. Meir's wife, was his daughter; see there. Semachot, end of chapter 12, and Eikhah Midrash, on “He ground my teeth with gravel”: R. Chananyah ben Teradyon's son went astray; robbers seized and killed him. He was found swollen after three days. They treated him honorably, placed him on a bier, and brought him into the town, praising him out of respect for his father and mother. The aforementioned Rabbah reads: he joined robbers, disclosed their secret, and they killed him and filled his mouth with earth and pebbles. After three days they put him in a basket and wished to praise him for his father's honor, but his father did not allow them. He said, “Leave me, and I will speak concerning my son.” He began, from Proverbs 5: “I did not listen to the voice of my teachers, nor incline my ear to my instructors. I was almost in all evil, in the midst of congregation and assembly.” His mother recited over him, Proverbs 17: “A foolish son is a vexation to his father and bitterness to her who bore him.” His sister recited over him, Proverbs 20: “Bread of falsehood is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be filled with gravel.”

(d) R. Eliezer ben Yaakov said: a person should not give a coin to charity unless someone like R. Chanina ben Teradyon is appointed over it—Bava Batra 10b; Avodah Zarah 17b. In R. Eliezer's name: Yoma 78b. R. Elazar ben Perata; see there. R. Chalafta, R. Yosi's father, was his colleague: Mishnah Taanit 15b, “In the days of R. Chalafta and R. Chananyah ben Teradyon.” And R. Nechemyah. R. Yochanan ben Zakkai, his colleague; see there. This requires investigation: he spoke in R. Eliezer's name, who was R. Yochanan ben Zakkai's student, and went to visit R. Yosi ben Kisma. R. Perata lived in his time.

(e) Gilgulei Neshamot writes: Jephthah's daughter is Ham's wife, who was pregnant with Sihon in the ark after illicit intercourse; see part 1 above, in Noah's generation. When she now came in this reincarnation for her repair, many troubles befell her to repair her: she was slaughtered by her father. She was R. Chananyah ben Teradyon's daughter, he being Jephthah's repair, and was saved because she had already been repaired by her slaughter. When placed in a brothel, she guarded herself against sexual sin, unlike her earlier conduct. R. Meir saved her. That guard, who did as R. Meir wished, had a connection to that repair involving Ham, her first husband. End of quotation, letter bet. Letter yod writes: Jephthah is R. Chananyah ben Teradyon, who was burned. His wife was killed for not protesting his pronouncing the Name by its letters. His daughter was confined in a brothel. Of Jephthah it is written, “I have opened my mouth to the Lord and cannot turn back”; this was his pronouncing the Name. They were now repaired, for on this account he was burned for sanctifying God's name. His wife then was also his wife here: as she did not protest then, neither did she protest now. His daughter, killed unjustly, was now saved. End of quotation. R. Meir saw that she had not sinned and redeemed her, telling the guard to say, “God of Meir, answer me,” and he was saved. For the secret, see Karnayim, discourse 6, and Yalkut Reuveni, Bo: the executioner destined for the world to come in Avodah Zarah, chapter 1, was a soul impregnation from Moses's executioner, because Moses's sword turned back upon him. He sensed the matter and performed kindness by hastening that pious man's death, according to Gilgulei Neshamot. Chesed LeAvraham, spring 5, river 25: “The land is broad-handed”—רחב״ת—is the initials of R. Chanina ben Teradyon. Possibly he was caught in the husk of Shechem ben Chamor and therefore had to be killed to be purified. The source continues, “ובל״א דל״א,” an unresolved phrase: he was to emerge from Shechem; when he was killed, the holy spark flew forth.
